items.label: f03-flaky-test
items.front: How does the handbook want you to investigate a flaky test, and what fixes are ruled out?
items.back: Run the case alone and with its neighbors to find which dependency leaks (shared state, order dependence, fixed sleeps, swallowed errors, accept-any-status asserts). Never fix it by raising arbitrary delays or disabling the test.

items.label: f04-definition-of-ready
items.front: Astra handbook: when is a story 'ready', and what is explicitly NOT a readiness requirement?
items.back: User benefit understandable, current behavior recorded, observable acceptance examples, source/test entry points identified, prerequisites satisfied, data-policy ambiguities resolved. A list of files to edit is not required; split anything over one or two focused sessions.

items.label: f01-favorites-acceptance
items.front: Personal favorites: what should happen when Eve (Globex) favorites an Acme page, and when a page becomes unreadable for a former reader?
items.back: Eve gets 404 and no membership row is created. The former reader's favorites list omits the page and does not leak its title. A join-table uniqueness test alone does not prove caller isolation.

items.label: f02-debugging-loop
items.front: State the debugging loop from the Astra handbook, in order.
items.back: Write expected vs actual; reduce the input or flow; find the last boundary whose output is correct; predict an observation that distinguishes your hypotheses; run that experiment; update the explanation, then fix. Afterwards remove instrumentation and record what evidence changed your mind.

items.prompt: Your PowerShell verification runner prints 'dotnet test FAILED' but the script finishes with exit code 0. How does the delivery handbook judge it?

choices.text: It only needs a finally block that restores the caller's directory
It is not a verification gate: check $LASTEXITCODE after each native command and exit with failure
It is acceptable as long as the failure text is visible in the log
It is fine because dotnet test already returned a non-zero code to the console

choices: It only needs a finally block that restores the caller's directory
It is not a verification gate: check $LASTEXITCODE after each native command and exit with failure
It is acceptable as long as the failure text is visible in the log
It is fine because dotnet test already returned a non-zero code to the console

items.explanation: 'A script that prints failures but exits zero is not a verification gate.' Capture/check $LASTEXITCODE after each native command.

items.prompt: A component test reports that a valid save request fails. Before changing production code, what does the guide tell you to check?

choices.text: The git blame of the save handler to find who introduced it
The production database, since the save may have been committed twice
The fixture: a fetch mock with the wrong method or path can make a valid request look broken
The CI logs, since local failures are usually environment noise

choices: The git blame of the save handler to find who introduced it
The production database, since the save may have been committed twice
The fixture: a fetch mock with the wrong method or path can make a valid request look broken
The CI logs, since local failures are usually environment noise

items.explanation: 'When debugging tests, check the fixture before changing production code. A fetch mock with the wrong method/path can make a valid request appear broken.'

items.prompt: Before starting your story, git status in the app shows modified files you did not write. What is the right first move?

choices.text: Inspect them and find out who owns them; do not discard them just to get a clean status
Reset hard to origin/main, since that is the canonical base
Commit them together with your story so nothing is lost
Run git restore on them so your branch starts from a clean tree

choices: Inspect them and find out who owns them; do not discard them just to get a clean status
Reset hard to origin/main, since that is the canonical base
Commit them together with your story so nothing is lost
Run git restore on them so your branch starts from a clean tree

items.explanation: 'If the project has existing changes, inspect them and determine who owns them. Do not discard them to make the status clean.' A separate checkout or agreed branch is preferable.

items.prompt: A release drops the Page.IsFavorite column and has a bug. Why does the handbook insist on discussing code rollback and data rollback separately?

choices.text: Because code rollback is always safe once the migration has finished
An older executable may not understand the new schema, and restoring a backup loses writes made since it was taken
Because data rollback is automatic whenever the code is reverted
Because SQLite cannot restore backups while the app is stopped

choices: Because code rollback is always safe once the migration has finished
An older executable may not understand the new schema, and restoring a backup loses writes made since it was taken
Because data rollback is automatic whenever the code is reverted
Because SQLite cannot restore backups while the app is stopped

items.explanation: 'Dropping Page.IsFavorite means an older executable may no longer understand the schema. Restoring a backup may lose writes made since the backup. A forward fix may be preferable.'

items.prompt: PageView.test.tsx with fetch stubs passes. Which claim does that test NOT support?

choices.text: That the component sends a request with the intended shape
That the UI is accessible for the tested controls
That a live server accepts the payload the component sends
That the component renders the stubbed response

choices: That the component sends a request with the intended shape
That the UI is accessible for the tested controls

items.explanation: The table: a component test proves 'Accessible UI and request intent' but does not prove 'A live server accepts the payload'.

items.prompt: Your tests passed locally and you opened the PR. What may you claim about CI in the PR description?

choices.text: That CI passed, since CI runs the same commands as your machine
Nothing yet: a local pass does not establish remote CI passed; link the actual run when available
That CI passed, provided git diff --check reported no problems
That CI will pass, as long as you add Closes #123 to the body

choices: That CI passed, since CI runs the same commands as your machine
Nothing yet: a local pass does not establish remote CI passed; link the actual run when available
That CI passed, provided git diff --check reported no problems
That CI will pass, as long as you add Closes #123 to the body

items.explanation: 'A local passing test does not establish that remote CI passed; link the actual run when available.'

items.prompt: You write a characterization test for behavior that is already correct, and it passes on the first run. What should you do?

choices.text: Break the production code briefly so the test is seen red first
Delete the test, since a test that never failed proves nothing
Accept it: a green first run is expected for characterization, so do not manufacture a red failure
Mark it skipped until a real defect makes it fail

choices: Break the production code briefly so the test is seen red first
Delete the test, since a test that never failed proves nothing
Accept it: a green first run is expected for characterization, so do not manufacture a red failure
Mark it skipped until a real defect makes it fail

items.explanation: 'If the task is characterization and the existing behavior is correct, a green first run is expected; do not manufacture a red failure.'

items.prompt: A test fires two conflicting writes with Promise.all and asserts only one wins. What is the handbook's objection?

choices.text: Promise.all rejects on the first failure, so the second write is never sent
Launching both together does not ensure they overlap at the database read/write boundary
Promise.all runs the promises sequentially, so it tests nothing concurrent
Concurrency tests must use fixed sleeps to be deterministic

choices: Promise.all rejects on the first failure, so the second write is never sent
Launching both together does not ensure they overlap at the database read/write boundary
Promise.all runs the promises sequentially, so it tests nothing concurrent
Concurrency tests must use fixed sleeps to be deterministic

items.explanation: 'Launching two promises with Promise.all or two tasks together does not ensure they overlap at the database read/write boundary.' Use explicit synchronization, and name a narrower test's limit honestly.

items.prompt: From the workspace root (which is not itself a repository) you run git status and it answers. What does the guide say that means?

choices.text: Git is reading the folio-app repo through a submodule link
The workspace root is a valid parent repo that tracks all sibling apps
Git created a fresh repository there automatically on first use
Git found some unrelated repository further up the directory tree, so you must not run git add from there

choices: Git is reading the folio-app repo through a submodule link
The workspace root is a valid parent repo that tracks all sibling apps
Git created a fresh repository there automatically on first use
Git found some unrelated repository further up the directory tree, so you must not run git add from there

items.explanation: 'The workspace root itself is not a repository; if Git answers from there at all, it has found some unrelated repository further up the directory tree. Do not use git add . or git add -A from the workspace root.'

items.prompt: A commit already pushed to a shared branch turns out to have a defect. What does the recovery table recommend?

choices.text: Delete the branch and recreate it from the commit before the defect
Interactively rebase the shared branch to drop the defective commit
Amend the commit and force-push so the defect never appears in history
Find dependent changes, then prefer a corrective commit or a deliberate revert over rewriting shared history

choices: Delete the branch and recreate it from the commit before the defect
Interactively rebase the shared branch to drop the defective commit
Amend the commit and force-push so the defect never appears in history
Find dependent changes, then prefer a corrective commit or a deliberate revert over rewriting shared history

items.explanation: 'Shared commit has a defect: Find its dependent changes -> Prefer a corrective commit or a deliberate revert over rewriting shared history.'

items.prompt: You staged a file by mistake but want to keep your edits in it. Which command fits?

choices.text: git checkout -- <path>
git restore -- <path>
git restore --staged -- <path>
git reset --hard HEAD

choices: git checkout -- <path>
git restore -- <path>
git restore --staged -- <path>
git reset --hard HEAD

items.explanation: `git restore --staged` unstages while preserving the working copy; `git restore -- <path>` (and checkout --) discards working changes, and reset --hard throws away everything.

items.prompt: Which test best matches the handbook's definition of a useful test for a rename permission rule?

choices.text: The rename handler's snapshot matches the previous snapshot
A Viewer's rename request is denied and the stored title is unchanged
The permission helper was called once during the rename request
The rename endpoint returns any status code without throwing

choices: The rename handler's snapshot matches the previous snapshot
A Viewer's rename request is denied and the stored title is unchanged
The permission helper was called once during the rename request
The rename endpoint returns any status code without throwing

items.explanation: A useful test fails for a plausible wrong implementation. '"The helper was called" is weaker than "a Viewer cannot rename this page and the stored title is unchanged."'

items.prompt: Search sometimes shows Installation results while the box says 'architecture'. Why does the guide make you reproduce two hypotheses separately?

choices.text: Because the browser Network tab can only record one request at a time
Because the debounce timer must be removed before either can be seen
An obsolete response overwriting the view and a failed query leaving old results are different mechanisms
Because each hypothesis needs a different database index to test

choices: Because the browser Network tab can only record one request at a time
Because the debounce timer must be removed before either can be seen
An obsolete response overwriting the view and a failed query leaving old results are different mechanisms
Because each hypothesis needs a different database index to test

items.explanation: 'a response for an obsolete query updates the latest view, or a failed query leaves previous results visible. These are different mechanisms.' Each gets its own controlled reproduction.
